sections.title: Variables and Assignment
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name pointing at a value. You create one with `=`, which is not equality - it means store this value under this name.

Read it right to left: evaluate the right side, then bind the name on the left.

Keep this to 3-5 sentences. If it needs more, it is two sections.

annotations.text: score now refers to the integer 42.
The right side is computed first, then stored back into score.

checkpoint._readme: A checkpoint gates the next section. It is a full Challenge but may omit id, xp and tags.
checkpoint.prompt: Assign the value 100 to a variable called `score` and print it.
checkpoint.explain: Assignment binds a name; print sends it to output. They are separate steps, which is why you need both lines.
checkpoint.hint2: The name goes on the left: score = ...

sections.title: Text and Numbers
sections.body:
Every value has a **type**, and the type decides what you can do with it. `+` means addition for numbers and joining for text.

Python refuses to mix the two, which is why `"Level " + 7` is an error and `"Level " + str(7)` is not.

annotations.text: Both operands are text, so + joins them: 23.

checkpoint.code:
x = "5"
y = 5
print(x + x)
print(y + y)
checkpoint.explain: The same operator does different work depending on the types either side of it.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 1 of 16 - code. Editor plus Run, graded by test cases.
guided-practice.prompt: Write a function `add(a, b)` that returns the sum of its two arguments.
guided-practice.explain: Returning rather than printing lets the caller use the result in another expression. A function that only prints hands back None, which is why print-based solutions fail the second test.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 2 - debug. Ships broken starter code; the tests must pass after the fix.
guided-practice.prompt: This should let its result be used in arithmetic, but the call crashes. Fix it.
guided-practice.explain: print shows a value to a human; return hands one back to the caller. Only one of those can be added to something.
guided-practice.hint: The function shows the answer but never gives it back.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 3 - output. Read the code, predict what it prints. Whitespace-normalised.
guided-practice.explain: Each line rebinds the name using its current value, so the multiplication uses 2, not the original literal.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 4 - fill. One input per ___ in the template; blanks are matched in order.
guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints the numbers 0 to 4.
guided-practice.explain: range(5) yields 0,1,2,3,4 - the stop value is never produced, which is the single most common off-by-one in Python.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 5 - order. Drag fragments into sequence; answer is the correct index order.
guided-practice.prompt: Put these lines in the order that defines and calls a working function.
guided-practice.explain: The body must be indented under the def, and the call has to come after the definition - Python executes top to bottom.

guided-practice._readme: TYPE 6 - explain. Free text, keyword rubric. layer is DECLARED because explain can be either.
guided-practice.prompt: This function is called a thousand times a second and memory keeps growing. Explain why, and what you would change.
guided-practice.explain: The list is module-level, so it outlives every call and is never trimmed. A bounded structure, or an eviction policy, turns unbounded growth into a fixed ceiling.

exam._readme: TYPE 7 - mcq. EXAM ONLY. Use only where writing code cannot test the idea.
exam.prompt: A function body runs to the end without hitting a `return`. What does the call evaluate to?
exam.explain: Python returns None implicitly. That is why calling a print-only function and using its result gives None rather than the printed text.

exam._readme: TYPE 8 - multi. EXAM ONLY. Every correct option is required.
exam.prompt: Which of these expressions evaluate to a string?
exam.explain: str(), concatenation and f-strings all produce text. Only the bare arithmetic produces a number.

exam.prompt: Write `clamp(x, low, high)` returning `low` if `x` is below it, `high` if above, otherwise `x`.
exam.explain: Returning early on each bound reads better than one nested conditional, and makes the inclusive boundary obvious.
range(1, 4) yields 1, 2 and 3 - the stop value is never produced.

exam.prompt: This crashes with a TypeError. Fix it without changing `level`.
exam.explain: You cannot join a str and an int with +. str(level) converts it; an f-string does the same more readably.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this returns the larger of two numbers.
exam.explain: Returning early removes the need for an else - once a return fires, nothing after it runs.

exam.prompt: In one or two sentences, what is the difference between `=` and `==`?
exam.explain: One stores, one asks a question. Mixing them up is a syntax error in a condition and a silent bug in an assignment.

exam.prompt: Order these so the program reads a number and prints double it.
exam.explain: input() always returns text, so the conversion has to happen before the arithmetic.

sections.title: Cost, Not Just Correctness
sections.body:
A correct answer that takes an hour is a wrong answer. **Complexity** describes how the work grows as the input grows, ignoring constants.

Linear search reads every element, so doubling the list doubles the work: $O(n)$. Binary search halves the remaining range each step: $O(\log n)$.

annotations.text: One pass over the input: the loop is the cost.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of `linear` above, and why?
checkpoint.explain: The worst case is the target being absent, which forces a read of every element.

sections.title: Reading a System, Not a Function
sections.body:
Larger problems are diagnosed rather than debugged. You are given symptoms and have to name the cause.

The skill is narrowing: what would have to be true for **all** the symptoms to appear at once?
sections.code: print("a system is a set of things that fail together")

checkpoint.prompt: A script gets slower on every iteration and memory rises steadily. Name the most likely cause.
checkpoint.answer: unbounded accumulation in a data structure
checkpoint.explain: Rising memory plus rising time together points at a structure being appended to and re-scanned each pass.

analysis._readme: TYPE 9 - complexity. A big-O answer plus written justification.
analysis.prompt: Give the time complexity of merge sort and justify it.
analysis.explain: There are log n levels of splitting, and each level does linear merging work, so the product is n log n regardless of input order.

analysis._readme: TYPE 10 - trace. Step through execution; each step is compared separately.
analysis.explain: One pass only guarantees the largest element reaches the end - which is why the algorithm needs n passes, not one.

analysis._readme: TYPE 11 - proof. Free-text formal argument, rubric graded.
analysis.prompt: Prove that the sum of two even integers is even.
analysis.explain: The whole proof is the definition applied twice and factored: 2k + 2m = 2(k + m), and k + m is an integer, so the sum matches the definition of even.

analysis._readme: TYPE 12 - problem. Mathematical problem solving, worked-solution rubric.
analysis.prompt: A list doubles in size whenever it fills. Starting from capacity 1, how many copies happen while inserting $n$ items? Show your reasoning.
analysis.explain: The copies form a geometric series summing to under 2n, which is why append is amortised O(1) despite occasional expensive resizes.

analysis._readme: TYPE 13 - scenario. Open-ended situation, rubric graded.
analysis.prompt: Your service is fine at 100 requests per second and falls over at 120. Describe how you would find out why.
analysis.explain: A cliff rather than a slope means something saturated. The useful move is measuring where time is spent before changing anything.

analysis._readme: TYPE 14 - diagnose. Named cause plus reasoning.
analysis.prompt: Every request works alone but half fail under load, with no errors in the application log. What is the most likely cause?
analysis.explain: Failures that appear only under concurrency, with a silent application, point at a shared bounded resource rather than at the request logic.

unseen-challenge._readme: TYPE 15 - design. No starter code, no hints - the engine enforces this on a design floor.
unseen-challenge.prompt: Write `Counter` - a class with `add(item)` and `most_common()` returning the item seen most often. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: A dictionary keyed by item turns counting into a single pass. Sorting the whole input instead would be correct but needlessly expensive.

exam.prompt: Time complexity of binary search, with justification.
exam.explain: Each comparison discards half the remaining range, so the number of steps is the number of halvings.
The search range strictly shrinks each iteration and cannot go below zero, so the loop must end.

exam.prompt: A teammate proposes caching every database read forever. Respond.
exam.explain: Unbounded caching trades a performance problem for a correctness problem and a memory problem at once.

exam.prompt: A sorted list search returns wrong answers only for the last element. Name the cause.
exam.explain: An exclusive upper bound treated as inclusive makes exactly the final element unreachable.
Two comparisons suffice for four elements, which is log2(4).

exam.prompt: How many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case for $n = 1000$? Show your working.
exam.explain: 1024 is 2^10, so ten halvings cover a thousand elements.

exam.prompt: Why is amortised O(1) not the same as O(1)?
exam.explain: Amortised is a promise about a sequence, not about any single call - which matters when one slow call would miss a deadline.

exam.prompt: Write `dedupe(xs)` preserving first-seen order. No starter code.
exam.explain: A set for membership plus a list for order is the standard pairing; using only a set loses the ordering the prompt asked for.

sections.title: What You Are Building
sections.body:
The boss floor teaches by building. Anything new it needs is taught here, in service of the project - never as a standalone lecture.

You are graded by the same runner as every other challenge: if the acceptance tests pass, it is done.
sections.code: print("read the spec, then build it")

checkpoint.prompt: State in one sentence what your program must do.
checkpoint.explain: Restating the spec in your own words is the cheapest way to catch a misread before you write code.

sections.title: Acceptance, Not Opinion
sections.body:
The tests are the specification. They are visible, they are not negotiable, and passing them is the whole bar.

Three harness modes exist: `function` calls a function, `cli` simulates argv and stdin, `file` checks what your program wrote.

checkpoint.prompt: What decides whether the boss project is complete?
checkpoint.explain: Nothing else counts - the harness runs your code and reports.

trial._readme: TYPE 16 - project. Boss only. harness is 'function' (implemented), 'cli' or 'file' (declared, stubbed).
trial.prompt: Build `word_count(text)` returning a dict of word to count, lowercased, ignoring punctuation. This is the trial: no starter code, no hints, acceptance tests below are the full specification.
trial.explain: Normalising before counting is what makes the second test pass; handling the empty case without a special branch is what makes the third one fall out for free.
